The gallery

Two pages, one skill pack, one rule bent twice.

frontend-design-pro is a skill pack an AI coding agent loads while it writes frontend code. These are two pages it produced, under briefs that asked for the same look. Both products are fictional. The repository README is the front door — this is where the output lives.

Earned

Bellwether A rehearsal tool for pending database migrations.

Its brief asked for near-black with one bright accent — the exact look the pack's own wall refuses to produce unless a brief asks for it. So this page was permitted before it was designed, and the question became what it had to do to be worth the exemption.

A cobalt at 55% lightness rather than an acid neon. One hue across every neutral. Every colour pair measured on all three of its surfaces rather than eyed — six pairs failed on the first pass and were fixed before it shipped. Density and one scroll reveal carrying the page, instead of a bright colour doing it alone.

Permitted

Nexus A fictional AI analytics platform.

The same exemption, taken and left there. Its brief asked for near-black and acid green and got exactly that: a WebGL hero, an asymmetric bento grid, a validated form, every constraint green, no rule broken — and a page that looks like every other generated developer-tool site on the internet.

It is kept here unchanged because it is the control. A gate can tell you a page broke no rule. It cannot tell you the page was designed.

Why a rule this pack wrote has an exemption in it

The pack ships a wall of AI-design defaults its skills will not produce. Three of them — cream and serif and terracotta, near-black with a single acid accent, broadsheet hairline columns — are banned unless the brief asks for them. Without that clause the rules would overrule the person using them, which is a worse failure than a generic page.

With it, a brief can walk an agent straight back into the default the wall was written to prevent. That is what the second page is: not a rule broken, a rule spent. The first page spends the same clause on purpose and has to earn it back in the parts no rule covers — chroma, measured contrast, density, restraint.

The difference between these two pages is not in any rule, and no gate in this repository can see it. Every constraint the pack enforces is green on both. That gap is the honest edge of what machine-checked design can claim, and it is why both pages are still here.

A concrete example, since the claim is cheap otherwise. The same wall lists Nexus by name as a brand not to invent, beside Acme and SmartFlow. Nothing in the constraint suite reads brand names, so the page carrying that name has passed every green run this project has ever cut. The other page's source names the same list in a comment and picks around it — the pack's guidance working at the moment of authoring, which is where it does its actual work, and nowhere a check could confirm afterwards.

Bellwether and Nexus are fictional products invented for these pages. Neither is a real service, neither collects anything, and no figure on either page describes a real system.

The pack is real: github.com/Krishna-Modi12/frontend-design-pro
